title: Depuis, pendant, il y a, pour

questions.q: « J'habite ici ___ trois ans. » (and I still do)
questions.why: Depuis is the one that means the action is still going on. Pendant would say it is over, and il y a would make it a point in the past.

questions.q: Which tense goes with « depuis » for something still true?
questions.why: English says I have lived here for three years; French says j'habite ici depuis trois ans. You still live there, so the action is present.

questions.q: Complete: « J'ai vécu à Paris ___ trois ans. » (and I don't now)
questions.why: Pendant is a completed span with a beginning and an end. French can even drop it before a bare duration: j'ai vécu à Paris trois ans.

questions.q: « Je suis parti ___ trois ans. » (three years ago)
questions.why: Il y a plus a duration means ago and needs a past tense. Depuis trois ans with the present would mean for three years, still true.

questions.q: Complete: « Je pars ___ trois jours. » (that's the plan)
questions.why: Pour is an intended duration, with verbs of going and coming. It cannot be used for time actually spent: j'ai vécu là pour trois ans is wrong.

questions.q: « Je ___ depuis trois ans. » (I haven't seen him for three years)
questions.why: Depuis normally takes the present, but a negative takes the passé composé, because the thing has not happened at all.

questions.q: Complete: « J'___ depuis vingt minutes. » (I had been waiting for twenty minutes) — verb attendre
questions.why: Shift depuis into the past by putting the verb in the imperfect. The whole frame moves back: I had been waiting, and still was.

questions.q: « Je pars ___ une heure » means « I'm leaving in an hour ». Which word?
questions.why: Dans is that much time from now; en is how long something takes. J'ai fait ça en une heure means it took me an hour.

questions.q: Complete: « J'ai fini le travail ___ dix minutes. » (it took me ten minutes)
questions.why: En measures the time an action consumed. Dans dix minutes would mean the work starts ten minutes from now.
The present tense with depuis is the whole point: I have been waiting for an hour and still am.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I've lived here for three years. (using ça fait)
questions.why: Ça fait … que, il y a … que and voilà … que are all equivalent to depuis, and all keep the present tense. Ça fait is the commonest in speech.

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — not equivalent to the other three?
choices: Il y a trois ans, j'ai déménagé.
Ça fait trois ans que j'habite ici.
Voilà trois ans que j'habite ici.
questions.why: The first is il y a as ago: one finished event, past tense. The other three are the depuis pattern: still true, present tense.

questions.q: Complete: « ___ lundi au jeudi. » (Monday to Thursday)
questions.why: Du … au marks a stretch from one day to another. Related markers: à partir de lundi (from Monday onwards), jusqu'à demain (until tomorrow), dès demain (as early as tomorrow).
Dans is time counted forward from now. Swap it for en and the sentence would claim the departure itself took ten minutes.

questions.q: English uses « for » for all four of depuis, pendant, il y a and pour. State what each one actually means and the tense it takes.
a: depuis — since / for, still going on; takes the present (or the imperfect for a past frame, or the passé composé when negative): j'habite ici depuis trois ans. pendant — for / during, a completed span; usually a past tense, and it can be dropped: j'ai vécu là pendant trois ans. il y a — ago, a point in the past; requires a past tense: je suis parti il y a trois ans. pour — an intended or planned span, with verbs of going and coming: je pars pour trois jours. Two questions sort them: is it still going on, and is it a span or a point?
questions.why: The tense is the giveaway. Depuis with a past tense, or il y a with a present, is almost always a mistake.
